items.readable_text:
Content:
For a curve defined by the parametric equations

Content:
[MATH: x=x(t), \quad y=y(t), \qquad t\in [a,b],]

Content:
the arc length of the curve between [MATH: t=a] and [MATH: t=b] is given by

Content:
[MATH: L = \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\,\textrm{d}t.]

Content:
Now, if we express our curve as a vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] as

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf r(t) = \left\langle x(t), y(t)\right\rangle, \qquad t\in [a,b],]

Content:
we can express the arc length of the curve in a more compact form as follows:

Content:
[MATH: L= \int_{a}^{b} \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm d t]

Content:
It's easy to see that this is equivalent to the original arc length formula. First, note that
[MATH: \mathbf r'(t) = \left\langle \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}, \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right\rangle.]
Calculating the magnitude of this vector, we get
[MATH: \|\mathbf r'(t)\| = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2},]
and thus the integral of [MATH: \|\mathbf r'(t)\|] with respect to [MATH: t] over [MATH: [a,b]] gives the arc length of the curve.

Content:
Finally, note that we can use this arc length formula to find a curve's length in two and three dimensions.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to calculate the arc length of the curve [MATH: C] given by the vector-valued function
[MATH: \mathbf r(t)= \left\langle \dfrac{t^3}{3}, \: \dfrac{t^2}{2}\right\rangle, \qquad t \in [0,1].]

Content:
The length of this curve is given by
[MATH: L= \int_{0}^{1} \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm d t.]

Content:
To compute [MATH: \| \mathbf r'(t) \|,] we take the derivative of [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] and compute its magnitude as follows:
[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= ⟨(d)/(dt)((t^{3})/(3)), (d)/(dt)((t^{2})/(2))⟩; = ⟨t^{2}, t⟩,; ‖r^{′}(t)‖|= sqrt((t^{2})^{2} + t^{2}); = sqrt(t^{4} + t^{2}).]

Content:
Therefore, the length of the curve [MATH: C] is given by the integral

Content:
[MATH: L|= ∫_{0}^{1}sqrt(t^{4} + t^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}sqrt(t^{2} ⋅ (t^{2} + 1))dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}sqrt(t^{2}) ⋅ sqrt(t^{2} + 1)dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}|t|⋅ sqrt(t^{2} + 1)dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}t ⋅ sqrt(t^{2} + 1)dt.]

Content:
We can solve this integral using substitution. Let [MATH: u = t^2+1,] then [MATH: \textrm d u = 2 t\,\textrm d t.] Therefore, our integral becomes

Content:
[MATH: L|= ∫_{0}^{1}t ⋅ sqrt(t^{2} + 1)dt; = (1)/(2)∫_{1}^{2}sqrt(u)du; = (1)/(2)∫_{1}^{2}u^{1/2}du; = (1)/(2) ⋅ (2)/(3)[u^{3/2}]_{1}^{2}; = (1)/(3)(2sqrt(2) − 1).]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Given a curve [MATH: C] parametrized by a function [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t)], we can approximate the arc length by breaking up the curve into many small line segments and adding up their lengths.

Content:
To do this, we first choose a finite number of points [MATH: P_0,] [MATH: P_1,] [MATH: \cdots,] [MATH: P_n] along [MATH: C] and form the polygonal path
[MATH: \overline{P_0P_1} \cup \overline{P_1P_2} \cup \cdots \cup \overline{P_{n-1}P_n},]
as shown in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7ae62e57a45ce32a8b87954961545122]

Content:
Then, we can approximate the arc length as the sum of the lengths of the line segments:

Content:
[MATH: L \approx \, \big\| \overline{P_0P_1} \big\| + \big\| \overline{P_1P_2} \big\| + \ldots + \big\| \overline{P_{n-1}P_n} \big\|.]

Content:
If [MATH: P_k] is at the tip of [MATH: \mathbf r(t_k),] then by the mean value theorem,

Content:
[MATH: ‖P_{k − 1}P_{k}^(―)‖|= ‖r^{′}(c_{k})‖(t_{k} − t_{k − 1}); = ‖r^{′}(c_{k})‖Δt_{k}]
for some intermediate point [MATH: c_k \in [t_{k-1}, t_k],] where [MATH: \Delta t_k = t_k - t_{k-1}.]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: L|≈ ‖P_{0}P_{1}^(―)‖ + ‖P_{1}P_{2}^(―)‖ + … + ‖P_{n − 1}P_{n}^(―)‖; = ∑_(k = 1)^(n)‖r^{′}(c_{k})‖Δt_{k}.]

Content:
This is a Riemann sum, and the closer the points [MATH: P_k] are to each other, the better our approximation will be. So, in the limit as [MATH: n\to\infty] (or [MATH: \Delta t_k \to 0),] we have

Content:
[MATH: L = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n} \| \mathbf r'(c_k) \| \Delta t_k=\int_{a}^{b} \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm d t.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
For a curve defined by the parametric equations

Content:
[MATH: x=x(t), \quad y=y(t), \qquad t\in [a,b],]

Content:
the arc length of the curve between [MATH: t=a] and [MATH: t=b] is given by

Content:
[MATH: L = \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\,\textrm{d}t.]

Content:
Now, if we express our curve as a vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] as

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf r(t) = \left\langle x(t), y(t)\right\rangle, \qquad t\in [a,b],]

Content:
we can express the arc length of the curve in a more compact form as follows:

Content:
[MATH: L= \int_{a}^{b} \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm d t]

Content:
It's easy to see that this is equivalent to the original arc length formula. First, note that
[MATH: \mathbf r'(t) = \left\langle \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}, \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right\rangle.]
Calculating the magnitude of this vector, we get
[MATH: \|\mathbf r'(t)\| = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2},]
and thus the integral of [MATH: \|\mathbf r'(t)\|] with respect to [MATH: t] over [MATH: [a,b]] gives the arc length of the curve.

Content:
Finally, note that we can use this arc length formula to find a curve's length in two and three dimensions.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Concrete Example

Content:
Suppose we want to calculate the arc length of the curve [MATH: C] given by the vector-valued function
[MATH: \mathbf r(t)= \left\langle \dfrac{t^3}{3}, \: \dfrac{t^2}{2}\right\rangle, \qquad t \in [0,1].]

Content:
The length of this curve is given by
[MATH: L= \int_{0}^{1} \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm d t.]

Content:
To compute [MATH: \| \mathbf r'(t) \|,] we take the derivative of [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] and compute its magnitude as follows:
[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= ⟨(d)/(dt)((t^{3})/(3)), (d)/(dt)((t^{2})/(2))⟩; = ⟨t^{2}, t⟩,; ‖r^{′}(t)‖|= sqrt((t^{2})^{2} + t^{2}); = sqrt(t^{4} + t^{2}).]

Content:
Therefore, the length of the curve [MATH: C] is given by the integral

Content:
[MATH: L|= ∫_{0}^{1}sqrt(t^{4} + t^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}sqrt(t^{2} ⋅ (t^{2} + 1))dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}sqrt(t^{2}) ⋅ sqrt(t^{2} + 1)dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}|t|⋅ sqrt(t^{2} + 1)dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}t ⋅ sqrt(t^{2} + 1)dt.]

Content:
We can solve this integral using substitution. Let [MATH: u = t^2+1,] then [MATH: \textrm d u = 2 t\,\textrm d t.] Therefore, our integral becomes

Content:
[MATH: L|= ∫_{0}^{1}t ⋅ sqrt(t^{2} + 1)dt; = (1)/(2)∫_{1}^{2}sqrt(u)du; = (1)/(2)∫_{1}^{2}u^{1/2}du; = (1)/(2) ⋅ (2)/(3)[u^{3/2}]_{1}^{2}; = (1)/(3)(2sqrt(2) − 1).]

---

Item 3 — Example: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Curve

Example Prompt:
Write down the integral that gives the arc length of the curve [MATH: \mathbf f (t) = \langle 3 \sin t, \: 2\sin 2t \rangle]
from [MATH: t =\dfrac {3\pi} 2] to [MATH: t = 2\pi.]

[IMG: /graphics/0c0c2dffe8d85c38943e919e899e3373]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we find [MATH: \mathbf f'(t)] and [MATH: \|\mathbf f'(t)\|\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: f^{′}(t)|= ⟨(d)/(dt)(3\sin t), (d)/(dt)(2\sin 2t)⟩; = ⟨3\cos t, 4\cos 2t⟩; ‖f^{′}(t)‖|= sqrt((3\cos t)^{2} + (4\cos 2t)^{2}); = sqrt(9\cos^{2} t + 16\cos^{2} 2t)]

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is
[MATH: L|= ∫_{a}^{b}‖f^{′}(t)‖dt; = ∫_{3π/2}^{2π}sqrt(9\cos^{2} t + 16\cos^{2} 2t)dt.]

---

Item 6 — Example: Computing the Arc Length of a Planar Curve

Example Prompt:
Find the arc length of the curve [MATH: \mathbf g (t) = \langle 3 - 2 \sin 2t, \: 1 - 2\cos 2t \rangle] from [MATH: t=\dfrac \pi 3] to [MATH: \pi.]

[IMG: /graphics/bfcb501a54f7ab19db15a4c4726f7f63]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we find [MATH: \mathbf g'(t)] and [MATH: \|\mathbf g'(t)\|\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: g^{′}(t)|= ⟨(d)/(dt)(3 − 2\sin 2t), (d)/(dt)(1 − 2\cos 2t)⟩; = ⟨ − 4\cos 2t, 4\sin 2t⟩; ‖g^{′}(t)‖|= sqrt((− 4\cos 2t)^{2} + (4\sin 2t)^{2}); = sqrt(16\cos^{2} 2t + 16\sin^{2} 2t); = sqrt(16); = 4]

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is
[MATH: L|= ∫_{a}^{b}‖g^{′}(t)‖dt; = ∫_{π/3}^{π}4dt; = 4t|_{π/3}^{π}; = 4(π − (π)/(3)); = (8π)/(3).]

---

Item 9 — Example: Computing the Arc Length of a Three-Dimensional Spatial Curve

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/3fca46c2b71edab0ded0e3d361c48c4f]

Find the arc length of the curve [MATH: \mathbf r (t) = \langle \sin t ,\: \cos t, \: t \rangle]
from [MATH: t =0] to [MATH: t = 2\pi.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we find [MATH: \mathbf r'(t)] and [MATH: \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= ⟨(d)/(dt)(\sin t), (d)/(dt)(\cos t), (d)/(dt)(t)⟩; = ⟨\cos t, − \sin t, 1⟩; ‖r^{′}(t)‖|= sqrt((\cos t)^{2} + (− \sin t)^{2} + 1^{2}); = sqrt(\cos^{2} t + \sin^{2} t + 1); = sqrt(1 + 1); = sqrt(2)]

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

[MATH: L|= ∫_{0}^{2π}‖r^{′}(t)‖dt; = ∫_{0}^{2π}sqrt(2)dt; = sqrt(2)t|_{0}^{2π}; = sqrt(2)(2π − 0); = 2sqrt(2)π.]

Item 12 — Tutorial: Deriving the Arc Length Formula

Content:
Given a curve [MATH: C] parametrized by a function [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t)], we can approximate the arc length by breaking up the curve into many small line segments and adding up their lengths.

Content:
To do this, we first choose a finite number of points [MATH: P_0,] [MATH: P_1,] [MATH: \cdots,] [MATH: P_n] along [MATH: C] and form the polygonal path
[MATH: \overline{P_0P_1} \cup \overline{P_1P_2} \cup \cdots \cup \overline{P_{n-1}P_n},]
as shown in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7ae62e57a45ce32a8b87954961545122]

Content:
Then, we can approximate the arc length as the sum of the lengths of the line segments:

Content:
[MATH: L \approx \, \big\| \overline{P_0P_1} \big\| + \big\| \overline{P_1P_2} \big\| + \ldots + \big\| \overline{P_{n-1}P_n} \big\|.]

Content:
If [MATH: P_k] is at the tip of [MATH: \mathbf r(t_k),] then by the mean value theorem,

Content:
[MATH: ‖P_{k − 1}P_{k}^(―)‖|= ‖r^{′}(c_{k})‖(t_{k} − t_{k − 1}); = ‖r^{′}(c_{k})‖Δt_{k}]
for some intermediate point [MATH: c_k \in [t_{k-1}, t_k],] where [MATH: \Delta t_k = t_k - t_{k-1}.]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: L|≈ ‖P_{0}P_{1}^(―)‖ + ‖P_{1}P_{2}^(―)‖ + … + ‖P_{n − 1}P_{n}^(―)‖; = ∑_(k = 1)^(n)‖r^{′}(c_{k})‖Δt_{k}.]

Content:
This is a Riemann sum, and the closer the points [MATH: P_k] are to each other, the better our approximation will be. So, in the limit as [MATH: n\to\infty] (or [MATH: \Delta t_k \to 0),] we have

Content:
[MATH: L = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n} \| \mathbf r'(c_k) \| \Delta t_k=\int_{a}^{b} \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm d t.]
